label: Isometric Immersions
notes: Chapter six, printed pages 124 to 143, studies a Riemannian manifold sitting isometrically inside a larger one. The central question is how the intrinsic geometry of the submanifold relates to the way it bends inside the ambient space, captured by the second fundamental form.

label: Immersions and the Metric
notes: An immersion has injective differential, so the ambient metric pulls back to a metric on the source. Locally the submanifold splits each ambient tangent space into tangent and normal parts, and this orthogonal decomposition is the engine driving every formula in the chapter.

label: Splitting the Connection
notes: Extend tangent fields to the ambient space and apply its Levi-Civita connection. Projecting the result onto the tangent space recovers the induced connection, while the leftover normal component is new information measuring how the submanifold curves away from flatness inside the ambient manifold.

label: The Second Fundamental Form
notes: The normal part of the ambient derivative defines the second fundamental form B, a symmetric bilinear map sending two tangent vectors to a normal vector. Symmetry follows from the torsion-free ambient connection, and B vanishes exactly when the submanifold is totally geodesic.

label: The Shape Operator
notes: Fixing a unit normal converts the second fundamental form into a self-adjoint shape operator on the tangent space. The Weingarten equation shows this operator is minus the tangential rate of change of the normal field, so it records how the normal tilts as you move.

label: Gauss Equation
notes: The Gauss equation expresses the ambient sectional curvature in terms of the intrinsic curvature plus quadratic terms in the second fundamental form. This is the precise algebraic statement of how bending creates intrinsic curvature, generalizing the Theorema Egregium of classical surface theory.

label: Codazzi Equation
notes: The Codazzi equation governs the tangential derivative of the second fundamental form. It states that the normal component of the ambient curvature equals the difference of covariant derivatives of B, providing the integrability condition that the tangential bending data must satisfy.

label: Normal Connection and Ricci
notes: The normal bundle carries its own metric-compatible connection, and its curvature is measured by the Ricci equation. This equation links the normal curvature, the ambient curvature, and commutators of the shape operators, completing the trio of fundamental equations that govern an isometric immersion locally.

label: Principal and Gaussian Curvature
notes: Eigenvalues of the shape operator are the principal curvatures, and the eigendirections are the principal directions. Their product is the Gaussian curvature and their average is the mean curvature. For a hypersurface these few scalars completely summarize the entire second fundamental form at a single point.

label: Mean Curvature and Minimal
notes: The mean curvature vector is the normalized trace of the second fundamental form across an orthonormal tangent frame. Submanifolds with vanishing mean curvature are called minimal: they are critical points of the area functional. Soap films model this condition, balancing surface tension equally in all tangent directions.

label: Totally Geodesic Submanifolds
notes: When the second fundamental form vanishes identically the immersion is totally geodesic, and geodesics of the submanifold are geodesics of the ambient space. Great circles on spheres and linear subspaces in Euclidean space are the model examples of this rigidity.

label: Synthesis
notes: Gauss, Codazzi, and Ricci together encode all the local geometry an isometric immersion can have. They split ambient curvature into intrinsic curvature, the bending of the tangent bundle, and the twisting of the normal bundle, unifying the chapter into one structural picture.
